newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr flat, but consumers perk up.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr flat, but consumers perk up.

text.p: The Australian dollar endured another flat session Wednesday as a longed-for surge in samurai demand failed to materialise, leaving the market lifeless.

There was some encouragement for those hoping the domestic easing cycle had ended as survey data showed consumer confidence had soared following the rate cut on November 6, so fulfilling one of the express aims of the RBA when it sanctioned the move.

Whether or not the Reserve Bank cut in three months time could not, however, generate the sort of electricity needed to stir the range-bound market and dealers feared the currency could linger in the recent US$0.7860/7910 band a few days yet.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was gathering dust at US$0.7882/87 after barely stirring from an early US$0.7874/79 and US$0.7880/85 late here Tuesday.

Immediate support was lined up at US$0.7865 and traders reported good bids from corporates around US$0.7820/30, while offers were thick at 79 cents, perhaps related to a rumoured strangle option. On the wide, a clear break of US$0.7810 or US$0.7940 was needed to signal a fresh trend.
On the crosses, it nudged up to 87.98/08 yen from 87.67/77 late Tuesday thanks to talk of samurai-related demand in the pipeline although the actual bonds were tardy in appearing.
There was some relief from A$ bulls that the U.S. dollar managed a modest rally to 111.65 yen after threatening to break below 110.00 earlier in the week.

However, they could not be sure the currency had bottomed until Japan and the U.S. made their thinking on US$/yen clearer. Both dollars were lifted by comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.

He said the U.S. currency was on its way back up and he always welcomed the currency's return to correct levels. That prompted some profit-taking on the mark's recent rise and helped the local unit to 1.1881/91 marks from 1.1779/91 late Tuesday.
In trade weighted terms the local dollar inched up to 58.0 from a previous 57.9 finish.
On the domestic front, the Westpac/Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index leapt 8.3 percent in November, ending four months of decline in dramatic fashion.

"Consumer sentiment has rebounded strongly in response to good news on inflation and the Reserve Bank's decision to cut interest rates (on November 6)," said Bill Evans, Westpac's General Manager, Economics.
Evans said this was the strongest immediate response to a rate cut recorded since March 1991.
This was not enough on its own to greatly reduce the risk of another rate cut -- that would depend on how wages, inflation and business investment fared in the next few months.
Nevertheless, it did meet one of the RBA's objectives when the central bank announced the cut.
Then it noted the easing would have taken mortgage rates to their low-point of mid-1994 which should "provide increased impetus to spending and confidence."
Thus if the improvement in sentiment bore fruit in higher consumer spending, another easing might not be needed.
